sources.cite: Amazon RDS User Guide: Restoring a DB instance to a specified time
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-14 (no last-updated date shown). Relevant text: 'You can restore a DB instance to a specific point in time, creating a new DB instance without modifying the source DB instance'; 'RDS uploads transaction logs for DB instances to Amazon S3 every five minutes'; LatestRestorableTime is read with describe-db-instances; 'You can restore to any point in time within your backup retention period'; on restore 'you can choose the default virtual private cloud (VPC) security group. Or you can apply a custom VPC security group'; 'Restored DB instances are automatically associated with the default DB parameter and option groups.' The page does not say how long a restore takes; the scenario's 30 minutes is authored.

brief.situation: You are the CloudOps engineer for Larkspur Goods, a fictional online store. At 14:00 support reports that every open order shows as cancelled. A schema migration ran against the RDS for PostgreSQL instance orders-prod a few minutes ago. Customers keep ordering, a refund worker refunds cancelled orders every 10 minutes, and the courier pickup at 15:30 ships whatever is open.
handover: Requirements: no order placed after the incident may be lost (RPO 5 minutes); statuses right before the 15:30 pickup; no spare database left running.
Automated backups are on with a 7-day retention; the repair host reaches databases in the orders-db-sg security group.
howItWorks: The board shows production, the restored instance and the workers; meters show refunds and lost orders.
Each task takes your time: start it, then let the work finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. Restores and repairs finish later on the same clock.
When you close the incident, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the record: what happened and when, how you chose the restore point and method against RPO and RTO, and what it cost.

parts.label: What and when
parts.criteria: Names the UPDATE without WHERE at 13:52:10 from the job log, and stops the refund worker that was turning bad data into refunds.
parts.modelAnswer: A migration ran UPDATE orders SET status = 'cancelled' with no WHERE at 13:52:10. The refund worker was refunding every cancelled order, so I paused it first.

parts.label: Restore point and method
parts.criteria: Restores to just before the change (not the latest restorable time or the snapshot) as a new instance with the right security group, and repairs only the affected column so no orders after 13:51 are lost (RPO) before the 15:30 pickup (RTO).
parts.modelAnswer: Point-in-time restore to 13:51:00 into a new instance with orders-db-sg, then copy the status column back for the affected rows. Switching to the copy would have lost every order since 13:51; the 04:00 snapshot would have lost ten hours of status changes; the latest restorable time already had the bad UPDATE.

parts.label: Cost and follow-up
parts.criteria: Deletes the temporary instance after a final snapshot, verifies counts and resumes refunds; proposes a guard (reviewed migrations, a WHERE check, or testing on a copy).
parts.modelAnswer: Counts verified against the morning report, refunds resumed, orders-pitr deleted after a final snapshot so it stops billing. Migrations now run against a restored copy first and are reviewed for unbounded UPDATEs.

expertPath.text: Pause the refund worker; the job log gives 13:52:10, and LatestRestorableTime is already after it.
Point-in-time restore to 13:51:00 as a new instance with orders-db-sg; it takes about 30 minutes.
Copy the status column back for the affected orders, check counts, resume refunds, delete the copy after a final snapshot.

restored.headline: Good: to the minute, nothing lost
restored.body: You stopped the damage spreading, used the log to pick the restore point, and repaired only what was broken, so neither the RPO nor the pickup suffered and the temporary instance stopped billing.

restoredGaps.headline: Repaired, with gaps
restoredGaps.body: The orders are right again. The criteria show what went out, what was skipped, or what the record gets wrong.

dataLost.headline: The recovery lost data
dataLost.body: Switching to the copy discards every order since its restore point, and a snapshot is hours old. A point-in-time restore to a new instance lets you copy back only what the bad statement changed.

pickupMissed.headline: Too slow for the pickup
pickupMissed.body: The latest restorable time was already after the UPDATE. Reading the log first gives the restore point once, and a restore costs about 30 minutes each time.

refundStorm.headline: Refunds went out
refundStorm.body: While the data was wrong, a worker kept acting on it. Stopping the damage comes before the repair.

notRepaired.headline: Still broken
notRepaired.body: The orders are still cancelled. A point-in-time restore never changes the source instance; something has to copy the data back.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Pause the refund worker first: it refunds every cancelled order. The migration log shows the UPDATE without a WHERE clause committed at 13:52:10; LatestRestorableTime (13:57) is after it and the 04:00 snapshot is ten hours older, so restore to 13:51:00. A point-in-time restore creates a new instance and never changes the source; give it the production security group (the default one blocks the repair host). Copy the status column back for the affected orders so orders placed since 13:51 are kept (RPO), finishing before the 15:30 pickup (RTO). Verify counts, resume refunds and delete the temporary instance after a final snapshot (cost).
